questions.question: What is inheritance in Java and how do you implement it?
questions.title: Inheritance in Java with extends Keyword
questions.direct_answer: **Inheritance** lets a **child (sub) class** acquire the fields and methods of a **parent (super) class** using the `extends` keyword, then add or override behavior. It models an **IS-A** relationship (`Dog extends Animal` — a dog *is an* animal) and promotes **code reuse**. Java supports single, multilevel, and hierarchical inheritance — but **not** multiple inheritance through classes.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can implement inheritance with extends and know it's an IS-A relationship aimed at reuse and polymorphism.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using inheritance just to reuse code when the IS-A relationship doesn't truly hold.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Run the IS-A test before using extends, mention @Override and super, and note Java has no multiple inheritance of classes.

sections.title: Inheritance: Reusing One Class's Code Inside Another
sections.content:
**Inheritance** lets one class reuse the fields and methods of another class instead of rewriting them. You write the shared code once, and other classes pick it up automatically.

The class that shares its code is the **parent class** (also called the superclass). The class that receives it is the **child class** (or subclass). You connect them with the `extends` keyword: `class Dog extends Animal`. Now `Dog` starts with everything `Animal` has — every non-private field and method — and can add new members of its own or **override** inherited ones to change their behaviour.

Why does this exist? To stop you copying the same code into every class. If `eat()` lives in `Animal`, then `Dog`, `Cat`, and `Bird` all get it for free — fix a bug once and every subclass is fixed. The second payoff is **polymorphism**: an `Animal` variable can point to a `Dog`, and Java calls the `Dog` version of an overridden method at runtime.

Java supports **three forms**, all flowing from parent down to child:

- **Single** — one child, one parent (`Dog extends Animal`).
- **Multilevel** — a chain (`GoldenRetriever extends Dog extends Animal`).
- **Hierarchical** — many children sharing a parent (both `Dog` and `Cat` extend `Animal`).

What interviewers really want, though, is the **IS-A test**: say the relationship out loud before using `extends`. 'A dog is an animal' is true, so inheritance fits. 'A car is an engine' is false — a car *has* an engine — so that should be composition, not inheritance.

The gotcha to remember: Java does not let one class extend two parents. That would trigger the **diamond problem**, where two parents could supply conflicting versions of the same method and the compiler couldn't choose.

> **Rule:** a class can `extends` only one parent — for multiple inheritance of type you use an `interface` instead.

sections.title: Single, Multilevel, and Hierarchical Inheritance
sections.content:
The three forms Java supports all flow downward — children extend parents, never the other way round. ```mermaid flowchart TD Animal["Animal
eat() · sound()"] --> Dog["Dog
sound() → Woof"] Animal --> Cat["Cat
sound() → Meow"] Animal --> Bird["Bird
sound() → Tweet"] Dog --> GoldenRetriever["GoldenRetriever
fetch()"] style Animal fill:#f5a623,color:#000 style Dog fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff style Cat fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff style Bird fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff style GoldenRetriever fill:#7ed321,color:#000 ``` `Animal → Dog` and `Animal → Cat` are **hierarchical** (two children, one parent). `Animal → Dog → GoldenRetriever` is **multilevel** (a chain of three). Every arrow means the child gets the parent's accessible members plus anything it adds itself.

sections.title: Implementing Inheritance — Animal and Dog
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using `extends` just for code reuse when IS-A doesn't hold** — you inherit the parent's entire public API, including methods that make no sense on the child, and lock yourself into a rigid hierarchy that's painful to change later.
- **Forgetting `@Override` on an overridden method** — a small typo in the signature silently creates a brand-new method instead of overriding, so the parent's version still runs and the compiler never warns you.
- **Skipping `super(args)` in the subclass constructor** — when the parent has only a parameterized constructor, the compiler's implicit `super()` call fails and you get a confusing 'no default constructor' error.
- **Trying to extend two classes** — Java forbids it because of the diamond problem; reach for interfaces when you need a class to take on multiple types.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`extends`** connects child to parent; the child gets all non-private fields and methods.
- Models an **IS-A relationship** — run the sentence test before you use `extends`.
- Three forms in Java: **single**, **multilevel**, and **hierarchical** — no multiple-class inheritance.
- Use **`@Override`** on every overridden method; the compiler will catch signature typos.
- Call **`super(args)`** as the first statement in the subclass constructor to initialise the parent part.
- Enables **polymorphism**: an `Animal` reference can point to a `Dog` and dispatch the right `sound()` at runtime.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The whole point of inheritance is to **avoid writing the same code twice**. If several classes share behaviour — every animal can eat — you put that method once in a parent class, and any class that `extends` it picks it up automatically. The parent is the **superclass**, the child the **subclass**, and `extends` links them; the child gets all non-private members, can add its own, and can override inherited ones to specialise.

Before I reach for `extends` I run the **IS-A test** — I say the relationship out loud. A dog is an animal, so inheritance fits. A car is not an engine, it has one, so that's **composition**. People get burned skipping that test and using inheritance purely for reuse: you inherit an API that doesn't belong and a rigid hierarchy that's hard to change.

The other payoff is **polymorphism** — an `Animal` reference pointing at a `Dog` still calls `Dog`'s overridden method at runtime. Java allows only **single class inheritance** because of the diamond problem, though a class can implement as many `interface`s as it needs. So my rule is simple: run the IS-A test first, and if it fails, reach for composition.

questions.question: Why does Java not support multiple inheritance for classes?
questions.title: Why Java Doesn't Support Multiple Inheritance
questions.direct_answer: Java forbids a class from extending two classes to avoid the **diamond problem**: if two parents provide a method (or field) with the same signature, the compiler can't decide which one the child inherits, creating ambiguity. Java keeps class inheritance single and unambiguous, and lets you achieve multiple inheritance of **type** through **interfaces** instead.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the diamond problem and that interfaces sidestep it (no instance state to conflict).
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying Java 'just doesn't allow it' without explaining the diamond ambiguity, or thinking interfaces don't have the same issue.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain interfaces avoid the state conflict, and for clashing default methods the class must override and use InterfaceName.super.method().

sections.title: Why a Java Class Can Have Only One Parent
sections.content:
Java does not let one class **extend more than one class** at the same time. You can write `class Dog extends Animal`, but never `class D extends B, C`.

The reason has a name — the **diamond problem**. Picture a grandparent class `A` with a method `greet()`. Two classes `B` and `C` both extend `A` and both override `greet()` differently. Now a class `D` tries to extend both `B` and `C`. When you call `d.greet()`, which version runs — `B`'s or `C`'s? There is no unambiguous answer. The shape this makes in a diagram — one top, two middles, one bottom — looks like a diamond, which is where the name comes from.

It gets worse than methods. The same **ambiguity** shows up across three kinds of inherited member:

- **Methods** — `B` and `C` each override `greet()`, so `d.greet()` has no single answer.
- **Fields** — if both changed a field from `A`, `D` would carry two conflicting copies.
- **Constructors** — the constructor chain could not be ordered cleanly through two parents.

To keep things simple and predictable, the designers made a class extend exactly **one** parent — one parent means one version of everything.

You don't lose the ability to be multiple types, though. A class can `implements` as many **interfaces** as it likes. Classic interfaces only had method signatures and no instance state, so combining two of them could never create a field conflict — the class itself provides the single implementation.

The gotcha interviewers love: Java 8 added `default` methods, which do have bodies. If two interfaces define the same `default` method, the **diamond comes back** in a mild form — the compiler forces the implementing class to override it and resolve the clash explicitly, picking one with `InterfaceName.super.method()`.

> **Key insight:** interfaces still can't hold instance fields, so the dangerous state-duplication half of the diamond never happens.

sections.title: The Diamond Problem — Why the Compiler Can't Choose
sections.content:
The shape below shows exactly why ambiguity arises. Both `B` and `C` override `greet()`, but `D` has two arrows feeding into it with no rule to break the tie. ```mermaid flowchart TB A["A
greet() — original"] A --> B["B
greet() — B's version"] A --> C["C
greet() — C's version"] B --> D["D extends B, C ??
d.greet() — which one?"] C --> D D --> Q["Ambiguous — Java forbids this"] style A fill:#f5a623,color:#000 style B fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff style C fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff style D fill:#e74c3c,color:#fff style Q fill:#c0392b,color:#fff ``` The diamond shape makes the problem visible: one root (`A`), two paths (`B` and `C`), one bottom (`D`). Java cuts this knot by disallowing the bottom of the diamond for classes entirely.

sections.title: Multiple Inheritance of Type via Interfaces
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Saying 'Java just doesn't allow it' with no reason** — interviewers want the diamond problem named and explained; the rule exists to avoid ambiguous method, field, and constructor resolution, not arbitrarily.
- **Claiming Java has no multiple inheritance at all** — it does, of *type*, through interfaces; a class can implement as many as it needs.
- **Assuming interfaces are immune to the diamond** — since Java 8, two `default` methods with the same signature clash, and the implementing class must override and resolve it via `InterfaceName.super.method()`.
- **Forgetting the real danger is duplicated state** — interfaces sidestep the problem only because they hold no instance fields; that's the insight that separates a good answer from a recited one.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- A class can `extends` only **one** class — to avoid the **diamond problem**.
- The diamond ambiguity covers conflicting inherited **methods**, **fields**, and **constructor chains**.
- Interfaces give multiple inheritance of **type** — a class can `implements` many.
- Classic interfaces have **no instance state**, so the field-conflict half of the diamond never occurs.
- Java 8 `default` methods can clash: the implementing class **must override** and resolve via `InterfaceName.super.method()`.
- The Java designers chose simplicity and unambiguity over flexibility at the class level.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Java caps a class at a single parent, and the reason is a specific headache called the **diamond problem**. Imagine a grandparent class `A` with a `greet()` method, two classes `B` and `C` that both extend `A` and override `greet()` differently, and then a class `D` trying to extend both. Call `d.greet()` and there's genuinely no right answer — `B`'s version or `C`'s? The same ambiguity hits fields if both parents changed an inherited one, and it makes constructor ordering impossible to define cleanly. So Java keeps class inheritance to **one parent**, which means one version of everything and no guessing.

What I'm careful to add is that this doesn't mean Java has no multiple inheritance — it has it for **type**, through `interface`s, and a class can implement as many as it wants. The reason that's safe is the part people miss: classic interfaces carry **no instance state**, so there's nothing to duplicate or conflict over.

Java 8 muddied that slightly with `default` methods, which do have bodies, so if two interfaces declare the same default method the compiler makes you override it and pick one explicitly with `InterfaceName.super.method()`. But even then interfaces still can't hold instance fields, so the dangerous half of the diamond — **duplicated state** — never comes back. That's the distinction I'd land on: **single class inheritance** kills the ambiguity, and interfaces give you multiple types without the state conflict.

questions.question: How does constructor chaining work with super() in inheritance?
questions.title: Constructor Chaining with super() in Java
questions.direct_answer: When you create a subclass object, the subclass constructor must run the **parent's constructor first** via `super(args)` — the **first statement**. If you don't write it, the compiler inserts an implicit `super()` (the parent's no-arg constructor). This guarantees the parent part of the object is fully initialized before the subclass adds its own state.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know super() runs first, the implicit super() insertion, and the failure when the parent has no no-arg constructor.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not realizing an implicit super() is inserted, leading to a confusing compile error when the parent only has a parameterized constructor.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why parent-first ordering exists (subclass code may rely on inherited state) and how to fix the 'no default constructor in superclass' error.

sections.title: Why the Parent Constructor Always Runs First
sections.content:
When you create a subclass object, the **parent class's constructor always runs first** — before the subclass constructor's own body. Writing `new Dog("Rex")` runs `Animal`'s constructor first, then `Dog`'s.

That's **constructor chaining**, and the mechanism is `super()`. Inside a subclass constructor, `super(args)` calls the matching parent constructor, and it **must be the very first statement** — no code can come before it. If you don't write any `super(...)` call yourself, the compiler quietly inserts a no-argument `super()` for you, targeting the parent's no-arg constructor.

Why **parent-first**? Because the subclass almost always depends on inherited fields. `Dog` uses the `name` field it inherited from `Animal`. If `Animal`'s constructor hasn't run yet, `name` is still `null` when `Dog`'s code touches it. Running the parent first guarantees the inherited state is ready and safe to use.

The chain doesn't stop at the immediate parent either. `Animal`'s constructor also calls `super()`, which goes **all the way up to `Object`**, the ultimate ancestor of every Java class. So the real order is `Object` first, then each ancestor down the line, and finally the class you actually instantiated.

The gotcha that catches almost every fresher: if `Animal` defines only a constructor that takes arguments and no no-arg constructor, the compiler's invisible `super()` has nothing to call. You get a *'there is no default constructor available in Animal'* error — and it shows up in `Dog`, even though you never wrote a `super()` call.

> **Fix:** add an explicit `super(name)` as the first statement in `Dog`'s constructor whenever the parent lacks a no-arg constructor.

sections.title: Constructor Execution Order — Who Runs First?
sections.content:
The chain always flows top-down: the topmost ancestor initialises first, and the class you called `new` on initialises last.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Caller
    participant Dog
    participant Animal
    participant Object

    Caller->>Dog: new Dog("Rex", "Labrador")
    Dog->>Animal: super("Rex")  ← first statement
    Animal->>Object: implicit super()
    Object-->>Animal: Object initialised
    Animal-->>Dog: Animal initialised (name = "Rex")
    Dog-->>Caller: Dog initialised (breed = "Labrador")
```

Notice that `Object` finishes first, then `Animal`, then `Dog`. Each level can safely use inherited state because the parent above it has already run.

sections.title: Compile Error — No No-Arg Constructor in Parent
Fix — Call super(args) Explicitly as the First Statement
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not knowing the compiler inserts an implicit `super()`** — when the parent has only a parameterized constructor, that hidden call has nothing to target and you get a 'no default constructor' error you never wrote.
- **Putting code before `super(args)`** — it has to be the absolute first statement in the constructor; anything before it is a compile error.
- **Assuming the chain stops at the immediate parent** — it actually runs all the way up to `Object`, with each level initialising before the one below it.
- **Forgetting why order matters** — if the parent ran *after* the child, inherited fields like `name` would still be `null` when the subclass tries to use them.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Every subclass constructor calls a parent constructor **first** — via `super(args)` or the compiler's implicit `super()`.
- `super(args)` must be the **first statement** in the constructor; no code can precede it.
- If you omit `super(...)`, the compiler inserts `super()` (no-arg) automatically.
- If the parent has **no no-arg constructor**, the implicit `super()` fails — you must write `super(args)` explicitly.
- Execution order is always **top-down**: `Object` → ancestor → … → the class you instantiated.
- Parent-first ordering ensures inherited fields are ready before the subclass body runs.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The key idea here is **ordering**: when you construct a subclass object, the parent's constructor always runs before the subclass's own body. The mechanism is `super(args)` — it calls the matching parent constructor and must be the **very first statement** in your constructor. If you don't write it, the compiler silently inserts a no-argument `super()` for you, which carries on up the chain all the way to `Object`.

**Parent-first** matters because the subclass leans on inherited state — `Dog` uses the `name` field that `Animal` sets up, so if `Animal` hadn't run, `name` would still be `null` when `Dog` touches it.

Where freshers get tripped up is when the parent defines only a **parameterized constructor** and no no-arg one. The compiler still inserts its invisible `super()`, finds nothing to call, and throws a 'no default constructor available' error that points at the subclass — even though you never wrote a `super()` call. The fix is just an explicit `super(name)` as the first line. So my rule is simple: if the parent has no no-arg constructor, **always call `super` explicitly**.

questions.question: What is the difference between IS-A and HAS-A relationships in Java?
questions.title: IS-A vs HAS-A Relationship in Java
questions.direct_answer: **IS-A** is **inheritance**: a subtype *is a kind of* its supertype (`Dog IS-A Animal`), implemented with `extends`/`implements`. **HAS-A** is **composition**: an object *contains* another and uses it (`Car HAS-A Engine`), implemented by holding a field and delegating. Run the IS-A test first; if it fails, model it as HAS-A.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can apply the IS-A vs HAS-A test to choose between inheritance and composition.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forcing an IS-A (inheritance) relationship where HAS-A (composition) is correct, just to reuse code.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note composition (HAS-A) is usually the safer default and that 'favor composition over inheritance' follows directly from this test.

sections.title: IS-A vs HAS-A: The Test That Picks Inheritance or Composition
sections.content:
**IS-A** means one thing is a kind of another; **HAS-A** means one thing contains another. IS-A points you to inheritance, HAS-A points you to composition.

**IS-A is inheritance.** A dog is a kind of animal, a circle is a kind of shape. You implement IS-A with `extends` for classes or `implements` for interfaces. The child inherits the parent's behaviour and can be used anywhere the parent is expected — that substitutability is the whole point.

**HAS-A is composition.** A car is not a kind of engine — it contains one and uses it. An order is not a kind of list — it holds one. You implement HAS-A by declaring the other object as a **field** and **delegating** to it: instead of inheriting `start()`, `Car` keeps an `Engine engine` field and calls `engine.start()` from its own `start()` method.

How do you choose? Run the **sentence test** out loud. 'A dog is a kind of animal' sounds right, so IS-A. 'A car is a kind of engine' sounds wrong immediately, so HAS-A. That one spoken sentence catches most mistakes before you write any code.

The interview insight is that **composition is the safer default**. It's loosely coupled — you can swap the `Engine` field for an `ElectricMotor` and nothing using `Car` notices — while inheritance is tight and hard to rework once the hierarchy sets. That's exactly why the Gang of Four advise 'favour composition over inheritance': don't avoid inheritance, just reserve it for when IS-A genuinely holds.

> **Default:** favour composition over inheritance — reach for `extends` only when the IS-A relationship genuinely holds.

sections.title: IS-A and HAS-A Side by Side
sections.content:
The diagram shows both relationships using familiar examples — notice how IS-A goes vertically (inheritance arrow) and HAS-A goes horizontally (composition field). ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph IS-A Animal["Animal
eat() · sound()"] -->|extends| Dog["Dog
sound() → Woof"] Animal -->|extends| Cat["Cat
sound() → Meow"] end subgraph HAS-A Car["Car
start() → delegates"] -.->|has a field| Engine["Engine
start()"] Order["Order
getTotal()"] -.->|has a field| Items["List of Items"] end style Animal fill:#f5a623,color:#000 style Dog fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff style Cat fill:#4a90d9,color:#fff style Car fill:#7ed321,color:#000 style Engine fill:#9b59b6,color:#fff style Order fill:#7ed321,color:#000 style Items fill:#9b59b6,color:#fff ``` IS-A uses a solid arrow (the UML inheritance arrow). HAS-A uses a dashed arrow (the UML aggregation or composition arrow). In Java code, IS-A is `extends`; HAS-A is a `private final Engine engine` field.

sections.title: IS-A vs HAS-A at a Glance
sections.content:
| Aspect | IS-A (Inheritance) | HAS-A (Composition) |
|---|---|---|
| **Meaning** | Is a kind of | Contains / uses |
| **Java keyword** | `extends` / `implements` | Field + delegation |
| **Example** | `Dog extends Animal` | `Car { Engine engine; }` |
| **Coupling** | Tight | Loose |
| **Flexibility** | Fixed at compile time | Swappable at runtime |
| **Sentence test** | 'X is a kind of Y' → true | 'X has a Y' → true |
| **Default?** | Only when IS-A clearly holds | Usually preferred |

sections.title: Wrong — IS-A Test Fails, Car Extends Engine
Right — HAS-A: Car Contains an Engine Field
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forcing IS-A just to reuse code** — like `class Car extends Engine`; you inherit the parent's entire public API, including methods that make no sense on the child, and leak its internals to every caller.
- **Locking yourself into a rigid hierarchy** — inheritance is fixed at compile time, so swapping the engine for an electric motor means reworking the class tree instead of changing one field.
- **Skipping the sentence test** — if you never say 'a car is a kind of engine' out loud, you miss the obvious signal that composition was the right model.
- **Treating 'favour composition over inheritance' as 'never inherit'** — inheritance is correct when IS-A genuinely holds; the advice is about defaulting to HAS-A, not banning `extends`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **IS-A** = inheritance (`extends`/`implements`); use when the child is genuinely a kind of the parent.
- **HAS-A** = composition (field + delegation); use when one object merely contains or uses another.
- Run the **sentence test**: 'X is a kind of Y' → IS-A. 'X has a Y' → HAS-A.
- Composition is **loosely coupled** and **swappable**; inheritance creates **tight coupling**.
- 'Favour composition over inheritance' (Gang of Four) — default to HAS-A unless IS-A clearly holds.
- Forcing IS-A when HAS-A is correct leaks the parent's API and makes the hierarchy hard to change.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
These two are really a **decision test for inheritance versus composition**. **IS-A is inheritance** — a dog is a kind of animal, a circle is a kind of shape — expressed with `extends` or `implements`, so the child can stand in anywhere the parent is expected. **HAS-A is composition** — a car isn't a kind of engine, it owns one — expressed by holding the other object as a field and delegating calls to it.

The way I decide is to **say the sentence out loud**. 'A car is a kind of engine' sounds wrong instantly, which tells me composition. People get into trouble forcing inheritance just to reuse code — `Car extends Engine` drags in the engine's whole API, exposes internals that make no sense on a car, and locks you into a hierarchy you can't easily change.

So my **default is composition**. It's loosely coupled — swap the `Engine` field for an electric motor and nothing using `Car` notices — whereas inheritance is rigid once set. That's exactly why the Gang of Four say favour composition over inheritance: not that inheritance is wrong, but that you reach for IS-A only when the type relationship genuinely holds.

groups.heading: IS-A (inheritance)
groups.text: A type that's a kind of another — a dog's an animal. You write it with `extends`. The child stands in for the parent.

groups.heading: HAS-A (composition)
groups.text: An object that holds and uses another — a car has an engine. You keep it as a field and delegate to it.

values: swap in a new part anytime

items: Pick IS-A only when the sentence test holds — 'a dog is a kind of animal' rings true.
Pick HAS-A when it's 'a car has an engine', or when you'll want to swap the part later.
Unsure? Default to HAS-A — it's loosely coupled and easier to change.

beats.text: `Car extends Engine` fails the test instantly. The fix: a `Car` holds an engine field and calls start on it. The **trap** people miss — forcing inheritance here leaks the engine's whole API into the car.
